lessons.title: Tensors: creation, shapes & operations
objectives: Create PyTorch tensors and reason about their shapes
Explain how tensor changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect tensor with shape and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A PyTorch tensor is like a NumPy array (as covered in the Data Science track) with two extras: it can live on a GPU, and it tracks operations for automatic differentiation. Getting shapes right is the single most common source of PyTorch bugs — most errors are a mismatched dimension somewhere in a chain of operations.
examples:
import torch
x = torch.tensor([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
print(x.shape)          # torch.Size([2, 2])
y = x @ x.T              # matrix multiply -- shape must align: (2,2) @ (2,2) -> (2,2)
print(x.dtype)           # torch.float32 -- most model math expects float, not int
commonMistakes: Mixing float and integer tensors, or mismatched shapes, and being surprised by a cryptic runtime error — always print `.shape` and `.dtype` when debugging, before anything else.
lessons.careerRelevance: Tensor shape fluency is assumed baseline knowledge in any PyTorch-based technical interview or take-home.

lessons.title: Autograd: automatic differentiation
objectives: Explain how PyTorch computes gradients automatically via autograd
Explain how autograd changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect autograd with requires_grad and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Every tensor operation with `requires_grad=True` is recorded in a computation graph; calling `.backward()` on a final scalar (usually the loss) walks this graph backward, computing the gradient of that scalar with respect to every tracked tensor automatically — this IS the backpropagation covered conceptually in the Deep Learning track, made concrete.
examples:
w = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)
y = w ** 2 + 3 * w
y.backward()             # computes dy/dw automatically
print(w.grad)            # 7.0  (since dy/dw = 2w + 3 = 2*2+3 = 7)
commonMistakes: Forgetting `optimizer.zero_grad()` between training steps — gradients ACCUMULATE by default in PyTorch, silently corrupting the update direction on the next step.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding autograd concretely (not just conceptually) is what lets you actually debug a PyTorch training run that isn't learning.
lessons.explain: Every tensor operation with `requires_grad=True` is recorded in a computation graph; calling `.backward()` on a final scalar (usually the loss) walks this graph backward, computing the gradient of that scalar with respect to every tracked tensor automatically — this IS the backpropagation covered conceptually in the Deep Learning track, made concrete.

lessons.title: Building a model with nn.Module
objectives: Define a custom model by subclassing nn.Module
Explain how nn.Module changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect nn.Module with __init__ vs forward and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A PyTorch model is a Python class inheriting from `nn.Module`: `__init__` defines the layers as attributes, and `forward` defines how data flows through them. This is deliberately just Python — you can use any control flow, print statements, or debugging tools you'd use in normal Python code, unlike more declarative frameworks.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to call `super().__init__()` in a custom module's `__init__` — PyTorch's internal parameter-tracking machinery silently doesn't work correctly without it.
lessons.careerRelevance: This exact class shape is how virtually every PyTorch model, from a toy example to a production system, is defined.

lessons.title: Datasets & DataLoaders
objectives: Wrap real data in a Dataset and load it efficiently with a DataLoader
Explain how Dataset changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Dataset with DataLoader and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A `Dataset` defines how to get one item (`__getitem__`) and how many items exist (`__len__`) — your data can come from anywhere (files, a database, a folder of images). A `DataLoader` wraps a Dataset to handle batching, shuffling, and parallel loading automatically, so your training loop just asks for the next batch without knowing any of these details.
commonMistakes: Loading an entire large dataset into memory in `__init__` instead of loading each item lazily in `__getitem__` — this defeats the purpose of a Dataset for data too large to fit in memory at.
lessons.careerRelevance: This Dataset/DataLoader pattern is the standard, expected way real PyTorch projects handle data, not just a toy convenience.

lessons.title: The training loop in practice
objectives: Write a complete, correct PyTorch training loop
Explain how training loop changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect training loop with model.train() vs model.eval() and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: This assembles the Deep Learning track's training-loop concept into real, runnable code: for each batch, compute the model's prediction (forward pass), compute the loss, zero old gradients, call `.backward()` to compute new ones, and step the optimizer to update weights.
examples:
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    model.train()
    for batch_x, batch_y in train_loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        preds = model(batch_x)
        loss = loss_fn(preds, batch_y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
    # then: model.eval(), compute validation loss with torch.no_grad()
commonMistakes: Forgetting `model.eval()` and `torch.no_grad()` during validation — this leaves dropout/batch-norm in training mode and needlessly tracks gradients, wasting memory and giving inconsistent.
lessons.careerRelevance: Writing this loop correctly from memory is one of the most common practical PyTorch interview/take-home tasks.
lessons.explain: This assembles the Deep Learning track's training-loop concept into real, runnable code: for each batch, compute the model's prediction (forward pass), compute the loss, zero old gradients, call `.backward()` to compute new ones, and step the optimizer to update weights.

lessons.title: Debugging PyTorch models
objectives: Apply a systematic checklist when a PyTorch model isn't training correctly
Explain how shape debugging changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect shape debugging with the overfit-10-examples test and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: When a model won't learn, work through a checklist rather than guessing: are shapes actually what you expect at each step (print them)? Is the loss actually decreasing at all, even slightly, on a tiny subset of data (if it can't overfit 10 examples, something is fundamentally broken)?
examples:
# the single most useful debugging step: try to overfit a TINY subset (e.g. 10 examples)
# if the model can't drive loss near zero on just 10 examples, the bug is in your code,
# not your model's capacity or the dataset's difficulty
commonMistakes: Assuming a bug is due to 'the model needing more data/epochs' before ruling out an actual code bug — the tiny-subset overfit test is a fast, decisive way to separate the two.
lessons.careerRelevance: This debugging checklist is precisely the practical skill that separates someone who's only followed tutorials from someone who can actually ship a working model.

lessons.title: GPU/device management
objectives: Move models and data to a GPU correctly and avoid device-mismatch errors
Explain how device management changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect device management with CPU vs GPU and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: PyTorch tensors and models must be explicitly moved to a device (CPU or GPU) with `.to(device)`, and a model and the data it processes must be on the SAME device, or you'll get an explicit error. Writing device-agnostic code (checking `torch.cuda.is_available()`) lets the same code run correctly whether or not a GPU is present.
examples:
device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
model = model.to(device)
for batch_x, batch_y in loader:
    batch_x, batch_y = batch_x.to(device), batch_y.to(device)
    preds = model(batch_x)   # now both model and data are on the same device
commonMistakes: Moving the model to a GPU but forgetting to move each batch of data too — this throws an explicit 'expected all tensors on same device' error, one of the most common early PyTorch mistakes.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correct device management is assumed baseline competence for training anything beyond a toy example.
lessons.explain: PyTorch tensors and models must be explicitly moved to a device (CPU or GPU) with `.to(device)`, and a model and the data it processes must be on the SAME device, or you'll get an explicit error. Writing device-agnostic code (checking `torch.cuda.is_available()`) lets the same code run correctly whether or not a GPU is present.
lessons.example:
device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
model = model.to(device)
for batch_x, batch_y in loader:
    batch_x, batch_y = batch_x.to(device), batch_y.to(device)
    preds = model(batch_x)   # now both model and data are on the same device

lessons.title: Saving, loading & deploying a trained model
objectives: Save and reload a trained model's weights, and describe the path to deployment
Explain how state_dict changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect state_dict with weights vs architecture and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: PyTorch typically saves just the model's learned weights (`state_dict`), not the whole Python object, since code can change between saving and loading — you recreate the model architecture in code, then load the saved weights into it.
examples:
torch.save(model.state_dict(), 'model_weights.pth')

# later, even in a different script/session:
model = SimpleNet()                      # recreate the architecture first
model.load_state_dict(torch.load('model_weights.pth'))
model.eval()                              # ready for inference
commonMistakes: Saving the entire model object with `torch.save(model, ...)` instead of just its `state_dict` — this can break if your class definition changes even slightly later, unlike loading weights.
lessons.careerRelevance: This exact save/load/serve pattern is the direct bridge from 'I trained a model' to a real, deployed product.
lessons.explain: PyTorch typically saves just the model's learned weights (`state_dict`), not the whole Python object, since code can change between saving and loading — you recreate the model architecture in code, then load the saved weights into it.

lessons.title: Common PyTorch pitfalls
objectives: Recognize frequent, specific PyTorch mistakes
Explain how zero_grad changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect zero_grad with gradient accumulation bug and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Forgetting optimizer.zero_grad() before backward() causes gradients to accumulate incorrectly across batches. Forgetting model.eval() during inference leaves dropout/batchnorm in training mode, giving inconsistent results.
examples:
for batch in dataloader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()   # forgetting this accumulates gradients across batches -- a real, common bug
    output = model(batch)
    loss = criterion(output, target)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
commonMistakes: Forgetting optimizer.zero_grad() -- gradients silently accumulate across batches instead of being computed fresh each time, corrupting training.
lessons.careerRelevance: These specific pitfalls account for a large share of real debugging time in PyTorch projects.
lessons.explain: Forgetting optimizer.zero_grad() before backward() causes gradients to accumulate incorrectly across batches. Forgetting model.eval() during inference leaves dropout/batchnorm in training mode, giving inconsistent results.
lessons.example:
for batch in dataloader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()   # forgetting this accumulates gradients across batches -- a real, common bug
    output = model(batch)
    loss = criterion(output, target)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

What is a PyTorch tensor?
options: PyTorch's core data structure, similar to a NumPy array but with GPU and autograd support
a synonym for a neural network layer

quiz.q: What does a tensor's shape describe?
options: the size of each of its dimensions

quiz.q: What does dtype specify for a tensor?
options: its data type, like float32 or int64

quiz.q: What does autograd do?
options: automatically computes gradients of tensor operations, enabling backpropagation

quiz.q: What does requires_grad=True do to a tensor?
options: tells PyTorch to track operations on this tensor so gradients can be computed for it later

quiz.q: What does .backward() compute?
options: gradients of a loss with respect to tensors that require gradients, via the computation graph

quiz.q: What is a computation graph, in PyTorch's autograd system?
options: a recorded graph of the operations performed on tensors, used to compute gradients during backpropagation

quiz.q: What does nn.Module provide when building a PyTorch model?
options: a base class for defining a model's layers and forward computation in an organized way

quiz.q: What's the difference between __init__ and forward in an nn.Module subclass?
options: __init__ defines the layers; forward defines how data flows through them during a forward pass
forward defines layers, __init__ defines data flow

quiz.q: What does a Dataset class represent in PyTorch?
options: a way to access individual data samples, typically implementing __len__ and __getitem__

quiz.q: What does a DataLoader provide on top of a Dataset?
options: batching, shuffling, and efficient iteration over a Dataset

quiz.q: Why shuffle training data between epochs?
options: shuffling has no effect on training
it prevents the model from learning spurious patterns based on data order, improving generalization
shuffling always slows down training with no benefit
shuffling is required by PyTorch's API and has no other purpose

quiz.q: What does model.train() do?
options: puts the model in training mode, enabling behaviors like dropout that should be active during training
evaluates the model on a test set

quiz.q: What does model.eval() do?
options: puts the model in evaluation mode, so dropout/batchnorm behave consistently for inference

quiz.q: What does torch.no_grad() do?
options: disables gradient tracking, saving memory and computation during inference or evaluation
deletes gradients from the model permanently

quiz.q: What is the 'overfit-10-examples test'?
options: a way to measure final model accuracy
deliberately trying to overfit on a tiny subset of data, to sanity-check that the model/training loop can learn at all
only relevant for very large datasets

quiz.q: Why is shape debugging particularly common in PyTorch?
options: shapes are never a source of errors
mismatched tensor shapes between layers or operations are a frequent, sometimes cryptic source of runtime errors
shape debugging is unique to TensorFlow, not PyTorch

quiz.q: What does inspecting gradients help diagnose?
options: issues like vanishing or exploding gradients, or layers that aren't learning as expected

quiz.q: Why write device-agnostic code in PyTorch?
options: it lets the same code run correctly whether a GPU is available or not, improving portability
PyTorch requires all code to be GPU-specific

quiz.q: What does moving a tensor '.to(device)' do?
options: transfers the tensor's data to the specified device (like CPU or GPU) for computation

quiz.q: What does a model's state_dict contain?
options: the model's learned parameters (weights and biases), without the architecture code itself

quiz.q: Why is model.eval() important before running inference on a saved model?
options: it's not important, eval mode is optional
without it, layers like dropout/batchnorm may behave inconsistently, giving unreliable predictions
eval mode only matters during training
eval mode deletes the loaded weights

quiz.q: What must you load alongside a state_dict to fully reconstruct a usable model?
options: the model's architecture code (the class definition), since state_dict only contains the learned parameters

quiz.q: What is a common consequence of forgetting optimizer.zero_grad()?
options: gradients from previous batches accumulate incorrectly with the current batch's gradients, corrupting training
this has no real effect on training

quiz.q: Why check tensor shapes when debugging an unexpected PyTorch error?
options: shapes are rarely the cause of real errors
shape mismatches between layers or operations are one of the most common, concrete sources of PyTorch errors
shape-checking is only useful for very large models
